explanations.explanation: Stones it is. The LORD tells Joshua to have the men take up twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan, carry them along, and set them down where they spend the night. Joshua's own words are that each man takes a stone upon his shoulder. I stamp cookies for a living, friend, so my shoulders just filed a complaint.

I get it, it's a river, so water feels like the obvious pick. But the LORD asks for something else: twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan. The men carry them to the place where they spend the night. Nobody in this passage is hauling a single jar.

Reeds would be a lot easier on the back, I'll give you that. But the LORD says twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan. Joshua adds that each man takes one upon his shoulder. You don't put a reed on your shoulder and call it a sign.

True. The LORD says to take the stones "from the middle of the Jordan where the priests were standing" (Joshua 4:3). So these aren't just any rocks from along the riverbank. They come from that exact place, and that matters later in the passage.

This one's true, friend. The LORD says to take the stones "from the middle of the Jordan where the priests were standing" (Joshua 4:3). The spot is the middle of the river, right where the priests stood. No picking rocks off the bank and calling it a day.

Their children. Joshua says that in the future, when your children ask, 'What do these stones mean to you?' there will be an answer waiting (Joshua 4:6). Twelve big stones sitting there will get a kid's attention. Kids ask questions, and these stones are built to start the conversation.

The priests were right there in the river, so they already know what happened. Joshua says it's the children who will ask. He says, "…when your children ask, 'What do these stones mean to you?'" (Joshua 4:6). The stones are set up for the next generation.

Traders make a good guess, since they'd see a pile of stones and wonder about it. But Joshua doesn't mention any traders. He says the ones asking will be "your children" (Joshua 4:6). The stones are a sign among Israel itself.

No battle shows up in this answer, friend. Joshua tells them to say that the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant of the LORD (Joshua 4:7). Twelve stones are standing there because of a river that stopped, not because of a fight. The answer they give is about what the LORD did.

False is right. Joshua says to tell them, "The waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant of the LORD…" (Joshua 4:7). Nobody's bragging about a victory here. The stones point to the river and the ark, and that's the whole answer.

Memorial. Joshua says, "Therefore these stones will be a memorial to the Israelites forever" (Joshua 4:7). A memorial helps people remember, and these stones remember the day the waters of the Jordan were cut off. Big stones are good at that, because they're hard to lose.

A warning sounds serious, but that's not the word Joshua uses. He says the stones will be a memorial to the Israelites forever (Joshua 4:7). They look back at what happened when the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark. The point is remembering.

A boundary stone marks a line, and that's a fair thought. But Joshua calls these stones a memorial to the Israelites forever (Joshua 4:7). They aren't marking where anything ends. They're marking what happened at the Jordan.

The camp. The Israelites took up twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan, "and they carried them to the camp, where they set them down" (Joshua 4:8). That matches what the LORD told Joshua. Twelve stones, one per tribe, all hauled to the camp.

An altar is a natural thought, since stones and altars often go together. But this verse says they carried the stones to the camp and set them down there (Joshua 4:8). No altar gets built in this verse. They just set them down.

A city would be a long walk with those stones on their shoulders, friend. The verse says they carried them "to the camp, where they set them down" (Joshua 4:8). The city isn't mentioned here. The stones go to the camp.

explanations.answer: In the middle of the Jordan
explanations.explanation: Right in the middle of the Jordan. Joshua set up twelve stones "in the place where the priests who carried the ark of the covenant stood" (Joshua 4:9). So there's a second set of stones, and this set sits where the priests stood. And the writer says the stones are there to this day.

Mount Nebo is a whole different place, and this passage never goes there. Joshua sets these twelve stones up in the middle of the Jordan (Joshua 4:9). They go in the place where the priests who carried the ark stood. That's quite a spot to put stones.

The town of Adam isn't mentioned in this passage. The text says Joshua set up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan, in the place where the priests who carried the ark of the covenant stood (Joshua 4:9). So the stones go in the riverbed, where the priests stood.

The text says something different here. "The priests who carried the ark remained standing in the middle of the Jordan until the people had completed everything the LORD had commanded Joshua to tell them" (Joshua 4:10). So the priests stay in the middle of the river, not on the far bank. They're holding that spot the whole time.

False is right. The priests who carried the ark "remained standing in the middle of the Jordan" until the people had completed everything the LORD had commanded Joshua to tell them (Joshua 4:10). They don't wait on the far bank. They stay planted in the middle of the river.

explanations.answer: They cross over while the people watch
explanations.explanation: That's it. After everyone had finished crossing, "the priests with the ark of the LORD crossed in the sight of the people" (Joshua 4:11). The people go first, and the priests with the ark come last. Everybody gets to watch them make it over.

explanations.answer: They stay in the river overnight
explanations.explanation: The text never says anything about overnight. It says the priests remained standing in the middle of the Jordan until the people finished crossing (Joshua 4:10). Then they cross over "in the sight of the people" (Joshua 4:11). They cross once everyone else is done.

explanations.answer: They go back to the east side
explanations.explanation: Going back would be a strange way to finish, friend. The verse says that after everyone finished crossing, the priests with the ark of the LORD crossed in the sight of the people (Joshua 4:11). They cross over to the same side as everyone else.

Armed for battle. These tribes crossed over before the Israelites, "armed for battle as Moses had instructed them" (Joshua 4:12). Moses is the one who had directed Joshua. So these tribes are walking in with weapons, and they're doing it the way Moses told them.

The ark belongs to the priests in this story. The passage says "the priests who carried the ark" (Joshua 4:9), and they cross last (Joshua 4:11). The Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh go ahead of the Israelites armed for battle (Joshua 4:12). Different group, different job.

Flocks are a sensible guess for anybody on the move. But the text says these tribes crossed over armed for battle, as Moses had instructed them (Joshua 4:12). No sheep are mentioned in the verse. It's weapons they bring.
He exalts him. "On that day the LORD exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel" (Joshua 4:14). All Israel is watching it happen. I think that's quite a day for the new leader.
A crown is a big idea, but the text doesn't say that. It says the LORD exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel (Joshua 4:14). Joshua is lifted up in front of everyone. No crown gets mentioned.

explanations.answer: He gives him a new name
explanations.explanation: The verse never gives Joshua a new name. It says the LORD exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel, and they revered him all the days of his life (Joshua 4:14). Same Joshua, lifted up in front of everybody. And that respect lasts all his days.

Moses. The verse says Israel revered Joshua "all the days of his life, just as they had revered Moses" (Joshua 4:14). Moses is the one who had directed Joshua. So Joshua gets the same kind of respect Moses had.

Aaron was Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), but he's not the name in this verse. The text says they revered Joshua just as they had revered Moses (Joshua 4:14). Moses is the one who had directed Joshua. That's the comparison the writer makes.

Abraham, the man God called to start Israel's story (Genesis 12:1-2), is a big name, but he's not the one in this verse. It says Israel revered Joshua all the days of his life "just as they had revered Moses" (Joshua 4:14). Moses is the one who had directed Joshua.

explanations.answer: The waters return and overflow the banks
explanations.explanation: That's what happens. When the priests' feet touched the dry land, "the waters of the Jordan returned to their course and overflowed all the banks as before" (Joshua 4:18). The river that had been cut off is back to normal, banks and all. And the people had already crossed on dry ground.

explanations.answer: The riverbed stays dry until morning
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't give the river a night off. It says that when the priests' feet touched the dry land, the waters of the Jordan returned to their course (Joshua 4:18). It happens right then. Nothing waits for morning.

explanations.answer: The waters stand up in a heap again
explanations.explanation: The verse goes the other way. When the priests' feet touched the dry land, the waters "returned to their course and overflowed all the banks as before" (Joshua 4:18). The river goes back to flowing the way it always did. It even spills over the banks.

Gilgal. The people went up from the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month and camped "at Gilgal on the eastern border of Jericho" (Joshua 4:19). It's also where Joshua sets up the twelve stones. So Gilgal is the stones' new home.
Shittim isn't the name in this verse. The text says the people camped at Gilgal on the eastern border of Jericho (Joshua 4:19). Gilgal is the camp where the twelve stones get set up.

Bethel doesn't show up in this passage. The verse says Israel camped at Gilgal on the eastern border of Jericho, on the tenth day of the first month (Joshua 4:19). Gilgal is the place to remember, because the stones end up there.

True. "And there at Gilgal Joshua set up the twelve stones they had taken from the Jordan" (Joshua 4:20). These are the stones the twelve men carried out of the river. Now they've got a place to stand.

This one's true, friend. The text says, "And there at Gilgal Joshua set up the twelve stones they had taken from the Jordan" (Joshua 4:20). The stones that came out of the river get set up at the new camp. They're not left lying around.

Dry. Joshua says the fathers should answer, "Israel crossed the Jordan on dry ground" (Joshua 4:22). A whole nation walked across a river without getting their feet wet. That's quite a story to have ready at bedtime.
Holy sounds fitting, but that's not Joshua's word. He says to tell them, "Israel crossed the Jordan on dry ground" (Joshua 4:22). The ground was dry, in the middle of a river.

Level ground would be nice for walking, but Joshua doesn't say that. The answer he gives the fathers is, "Israel crossed the Jordan on dry ground" (Joshua 4:22). Dry is the word, and it's what makes the story worth telling.

Close, but that's not the sea Joshua names. He says the LORD dried up the Jordan "just as He did to the Red Sea, which He dried up before us until we had crossed over" (Joshua 4:23). So it's the Red Sea. The Sea of Galilee doesn't come up in this passage.

False is right. Joshua says the LORD dried up the Jordan "just as He did to the Red Sea, which He dried up before us until we had crossed over" (Joshua 4:23). The comparison is the Red Sea. Two crossings, and in both the water was dried up before Israel.

explanations.answer: So all peoples know His hand is mighty
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Joshua gives. He says the LORD did it "so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty" (Joshua 4:24). So this crossing isn't only for Israel to see. It's meant for all the peoples of the earth.

explanations.answer: So Israel could rest before the battle
explanations.explanation: Rest is a sweet thought, but Joshua never says it. The reason he gives is "so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty" (Joshua 4:24). That's what the text says the crossing is for.

explanations.answer: So the priests could reach Jericho first
explanations.explanation: The priests don't even cross first. They cross after everyone else has finished (Joshua 4:11). Joshua's reason is "so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty" (Joshua 4:24). Jericho's order of arrival doesn't come into it.

True. Joshua says the LORD did it "so that you may always fear the LORD your God" (Joshua 4:24). That's the second reason, right after the one about all the peoples of the earth. This one is for Israel itself, and it's meant to last always.

This one's true, friend. Joshua says the LORD did this "so that you may always fear the LORD your God" (Joshua 4:24). It's the second reason, right after the one about all the peoples of the earth. It's addressed to Israel.

Their hearts melt. When the Amorite and Canaanite kings heard how the LORD had dried up the Jordan, "their hearts melted and their spirits failed for fear of the Israelites" (Joshua 5:1). That's quite a reaction to a river story. The news about the Jordan reached them.

explanations.answer: They gather their armies to attack
explanations.explanation: The text shows the kings going soft, not marching out. It says "their hearts melted and their spirits failed for fear of the Israelites" (Joshua 5:1). No armies get gathered in this verse. The news about the Jordan shook them.

explanations.answer: They send gifts asking for peace
explanations.explanation: Gifts would be a smart move, but the text doesn't mention any. It says the kings' hearts melted and their spirits failed for fear of the Israelites (Joshua 5:1). That's their reaction to hearing how the LORD dried up the Jordan. Nothing more is said about what they do.
